claims.text: The substrate is Ti-6Al-4V in the standard wrought condition.
The proposed intervention is low-temperature plasma nitriding at approximately 600 °C for 8–12 hours in an NH3/H2 gas mixture.
Optimized plasma nitriding will form a thin, adherent, TiN-enriched surface layer on Ti-6Al-4V.
The nitrided layer will be continuous and a few microns thick.
The surface layer will contain TiN and may also contain Ti2N.
Nitrogen will diffuse into the surface region during plasma nitriding.
Diffused nitrogen will form hard titanium nitride phases.
The nitride phases will increase surface hardness by impeding plastic deformation.
The increased resistance to plastic deformation will reduce wear during sliding contact.
Optimization of nitriding duration and gas composition will prevent excessive layer thickness and associated brittleness.
The nitrided samples will exhibit surface hardness exceeding approximately 1600 HV.
The nitrided samples will have a markedly lower wear rate than untreated Ti-6Al-4V under comparable room-temperature sliding conditions.
The nitrided layer will retain adequate adhesion and toughness.
Untreated Ti-6Al-4V typically has lower surface hardness and higher room-temperature sliding wear rates than the proposed nitrided material.
The expected improvement is limited to room-temperature sliding tests, while behavior under high cyclic loading or elevated temperatures is not established.
The magnitude of improvement will vary with nitriding parameters.
A controlled comparison of nitrided and untreated specimens using reciprocating sliding wear testing, microindentation, XRD, SEM, and adhesion testing can evaluate the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness improvement, exemplified as greater than 30%, will falsify the hypothesis.
No reduction in wear rate relative to untreated controls will falsify the hypothesis.
Significant delamination or cracking of the nitrided layer during wear testing will falsify the hypothesis.
